label: Shofetim (Judges) — Part 3 — Chapters 15–21
summary_plain: Shimshon defeats the Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey — YHWH opens a spring from the rock. Delilah betrays Shimshon — his hair is cut, his eyes are gouged, he is bound with bronze chains. But his hair grows back. In the temple of Dagon, Shimshon pushes apart the pillars and the house falls on the lords of the Philistines. The closing chapters record the corruption at Dan and the civil war against Binyamin. The book ends: In those days there was no king in Yisra'EL — everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from 4QJudg-a, 4QJudg-b and the Orit Ge'ez. The closing refrain — 'there was no king in Yisra'EL, everyone did what was right in his own eyes' (17:6, 18:1, 19:1, 21:25) — frames the entire book. The absence of centralized covenant authority produces moral chaos. This sets the stage for the demand for a king in 1 Shemu'el 8 — and YHWH's assessment that the demand is a rejection of him.

key_terms.definition: In Shofetim 16, Shimshon falls in love with Delilah, a woman in the valley of Sorek. The Philistine lords each offer her 1,100 pieces of silver to discover the source of his strength. After three false answers she persists: 'You have mocked me these three times; tell me what makes your strength great.' On the fourth attempt he tells her about the Nazirite vow — his uncut hair. She lulls him to sleep, shaves his head, and calls the Philistines.

The key verse in Shimshon's story: 'He did not know that YHWH had left him.' After his hair was shaved, Shimshon woke and said 'I will go out as before and shake myself free.' He did not feel the absence immediately. This is the most chilling moment in his story — covenant absence can precede awareness of it. When YHWH's presence departs, the man continues acting as if nothing changed.

Blinded and enslaved in Gaza, Shimshon prays: 'YHWH my Creator, remember me and strengthen me just this once.' He is led between the two central pillars of the Philistines' temple during a festival. He pushes both pillars, the building collapses, and he kills more in his death than in his life. The text records that YHWH heard his prayer — covenant is restored at the moment of his greatest humiliation.

In Shofetim 17-18, an Efrayimite named Mikha builds a shrine with a carved image, makes an ephod and teraphim, and installs one of his sons as priest. He later hires a wandering Levite. The tribe of Dan steals the whole shrine on their migration north. The story demonstrates covenant breakdown: 'Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.'

Shofetim 18: the tribe of Dan had not taken its assigned territory and sent spies north to find land. They passed Mikha's house, stole his idols and hired priest, and settled in Layish (renamed Dan), destroying its peaceful inhabitants. The covenant failure is multiple: they never took their assigned land, they stole idols, and they destroyed a city YHWH had not given them.

The darkest story in Shofetim (ch.19): a Levite's concubine is gang-raped to death by men of Giv'ah in Binyamin's territory. The Levite dismembers her body and sends pieces to all twelve tribes as a call to judgment. The crime deliberately echoes the men of Sodom's demand in Bereshit 19 — Yisra'el has become what it was supposed to destroy.

In Shofetim 20, all Yisra'el assembles to demand justice for the Giv'ah atrocity. When Binyamin refuses to hand over the guilty men, war follows. Binyamin nearly defeats all Yisra'el twice before YHWH gives them the victory. Binyamin is reduced to 600 surviving men. The covenant community nearly destroys itself.

key_terms.term: 'Everyone Did What Was Right in His Own Eyes'
key_terms.definition: The refrain that closes Shofetim (17:6; 21:25): 'In those days there was no king in Yisra'el; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.' This is not a simple call for a human king — it is a covenant verdict. Without YHWH's direct authority acknowledged, without judge or covenant structure, human autonomy produces Mikha's idol, the rape at Giv'ah, and civil war.

In Shofetim 15, Shimshon kills 1,000 Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey at Ramath-Lehi. After the victory he cries out in thirst and YHWH opens a hollow in the jawbone and water comes out. The place is named En Hakkore — 'the spring of the one who called out.' YHWH provided in the moment of need after a miraculous covenant victory.

In Shofetim 21, after the near-annihilation of Binyamin, all Yisra'el had sworn: 'None of us shall give his daughter in marriage to Binyamin.' Then they mourned because a whole tribe was near extinction. They found a way around the oath through the virgins of Yavesh-Gil'ad (a city that had not come to the assembly) and through wives seized at the festival at Shilo. The book ends in moral chaos, bound by oaths they found ways to technically circumvent.

faq.question: What does 'YHWH had left him' mean for Shimshon's story?
faq.answer: This phrase is the theological center of the Shimshon narrative. Shimshon had been playing with the Nazirite vow for years — sleeping with Philistine women, touching a lion's carcass, attending a wine feast at his Philistine wedding. The final violation — revealing the secret to Delilah, allowing the sign of consecration to be removed — broke the covenant marker completely. YHWH's departure was not punishment imposed from outside; it was the natural result of the covenant sign being removed. The chilling element is that Shimshon 'did not know.' Covenant absence does not always announce itself. The person continues acting on the assumption that nothing has changed until some test reveals the absence.

faq.question: Does Shimshon's prayer at the end mean he was restored?
faq.answer: Yes — the text is explicit. 'YHWH heard his prayer' is the implicit affirmation behind his strength returning. His hair had grown back (noted in ch.16:22). His prayer is the first time in his life that Shimshon directly invokes YHWH by name in personal appeal: 'YHWH my Creator, remember me.' The vocabulary echoes Mosheh's intercession pattern. YHWH answers: the strength returns, the pillars come down, more Philistines die in one moment than in all his previous battles. His restoration in humiliation is the culmination of a covenant life that was always more capable than it allowed itself to be.

faq.question: What does the Levite's concubine story say about Yisra'el's moral condition?
faq.answer: The story is placed deliberately at the close of Shofetim as the bottom of Yisra'el's covenant descent. The crime echoes the men of Sodom — the host at Giv'ah even uses the same words as Lot's offer. Yisra'el has not driven out Sodom's spirit from the land; it has reproduced it in a Levite's host city in Binyamin's territory. The Levite's decision to cut up his concubine and send the pieces to all tribes is itself a horrifying act — both the call to judgment and the evidence of his own callousness (he slept while she died at the doorstep). The story is designed to shock: this is what covenant breakdown looks like at its worst.

faq.question: What is significant about the tribe of Dan's migration and theft?
faq.answer: The Danites had been given a coastal territory they never fully took. Rather than trusting YHWH for the land assigned to them, they went looking for easier territory. When they passed Mikha's house, they stole his idols, hired priest, and all, then settled in a peaceful northern city they destroyed without provocation. Their covenant failures are layered: failure to take their assigned portion, theft, false worship, unauthorized conquest. The idolatrous shrine at Dan persists into the period of the books of Kings as a site of ongoing covenant violation. The story shows covenant failure compounding over generations: one man's private shrine becomes a whole tribe's official worship.

faq.question: What does the civil war against Binyamin teach about covenant solidarity?
faq.answer: Yisra'el assembles at Mitspah — 400,000 men — in response to the Levite's testimony. The initial impulse is correct: a covenant crime demands covenant accountability regardless of tribal origin. Binyamin's refusal to hand over the guilty men forces a war Yisra'el did not want to fight. What follows is disorienting: YHWH permits Binyamin to defeat the coalition in the first two engagements, killing thousands of Israelites who were in the right. After the second defeat, Yisra'el wept before YHWH. Only after communal mourning does YHWH promise the third battle will succeed. The lesson: covenant justice is not automatically easy or swift. YHWH sometimes requires suffering even on the side of the righteous before the verdict is executed.

faq.question: What does the oath at Mitspah and its circumvention reveal?
faq.answer: The post-war oath — 'none shall give daughters to Binyamin' — was spoken in grief and later regretted. Yisra'el then mourned: 'one tribe is cut off from Yisra'el.' The 'solution' — taking the virgins of Yavesh-Gil'ad (a city that had not come to the assembly) and seizing women at the Shilo festival — is both inventive and morally bankrupt. The women of Yavesh-Gil'ad did nothing wrong; the festival-goers did nothing wrong. The book closes in a tangle of oaths that were technically kept while their spirit was violated, women seized without consent, and Binyamin barely surviving. This is what 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes' produces: creative solutions to problems caused by previous failures.

faq.question: How does Delilah differ from Shimshon's earlier Philistine connections?
faq.answer: Shimshon's first wife was taken because YHWH was using it to confront the Philistines. His connection to Delilah is presented differently — she is immediately revealed to be in Philistine pay, and Shimshon tells her three progressive falsehoods before finally disclosing the truth. He knows she is trying to betray him. He goes back to her anyway. This is not YHWH working through a flawed human impulse; this is Shimshon choosing known betrayal. The difference matters: the earlier marriages had a divine strategic element; Delilah is pure self-destruction. Shimshon's choice to disclose the vow is the one point in his entire life where he is fully responsible for what follows.

faq.question: What connects the ending of Shofetim to the beginning of Shemu'el?
faq.answer: Shofetim ends with the refrain 'there was no king in Yisra'el; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.' Shemu'el Aleph begins with Khannah's prayer for a son and ends with the demand for a king. The transition from Shofetim to Shemu'el is the transition from covenant self-rule (which failed) to covenant monarchy (which will also fail but differently). YHWH's response to the king demand — 'they have rejected me from being king over them' — frames the entire monarchy as a covenant concession, not a covenant ideal. Shofetim sets up why the people want a king; Shemu'el tracks what YHWH does with that demand.

faq.question: Why does Yisra'el mourn nearly exterminating Binyamin?
faq.answer: The mourning is genuine covenant grief: 'Today there is one tribe cut off from Yisra'el.' The twelve-tribe unity is a covenant structure established from Ya'akov forward. Losing even the tribe responsible for the Giv'ah atrocity is a covenant loss — YHWH's covenant people are twelve, not eleven. The mourning reveals something important about Yisra'el's self-understanding: despite the civil war, they know that Binyamin belongs in the covenant family. Their efforts to restore Binyamin's population (however morally problematic the methods) show covenant instinct working even in a moment of deep covenant breakdown. The desire to preserve all twelve tribes is itself a correct covenant impulse.

faq.question: What is the significance of Shofetim 15's water miracle?
faq.answer: The spring at Ramath-Lehi comes immediately after Shimshon's greatest single battle. He has just killed 1,000 men and cries out to YHWH in exhaustion and thirst: 'Now shall I die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?' YHWH opens water from the hollow in the jawbone. This is a small miracle sandwiched between the great ones. The covenant response to genuine need: YHWH does not leave his instrument to die of thirst after a covenant victory. The spring is named En Hakkore — 'spring of the one who called out.' Calling out to YHWH in need is itself a covenant act, and YHWH records the calling with a place name.
